title: We Make Ready Our Swords and Lances
intro: Ibn al-Iflili records that Sayf al-Dawla's mother died at Mayyafariqin. Al-Mutanabbi was in Antioch when the news came, and recited the elegy to the prince in Aleppo in 337 AH (948–49 CE). The poet begins with the weapons and horses people trust to keep them alive, then asks what use they are against death. The recording ends with a prayer that the rain over her grave may give as freely as her hand once gave.

translation: We make ready our Mashrafi swords and our lances,
and death kills us without a fight.
1.sharh: We can prepare for an encounter with another fighter. Death simply passes those preparations by. The poet never gets the battle for which the first half has equipped him.

translation: We tether our swiftest horses close at hand,
yet they cannot save us from the trotting nights.
2.sharh: He keeps the fastest horses where he can reach them. The passing nights become another horse, which has only to trot to catch whatever steed a man might ride.

translation: Who has ever lived without loving this world?
Yet there is no way to stay with her.
3.sharh: He speaks of the world as a beloved. Al-Wahidi takes the unattainable thing to be lasting union. One can possess the world's pleasures for a while, and that “for a while” is the heart of the grief.

translation: Your share of a loved one in life
is your share of a vision in sleep.
4.sharh: He measures the time one has with a loved one by a dream. Waking parts the sleeper from the figure he treasured a moment earlier, just as death parts people who were together in waking life.

translation: Time shot me with calamities until
my heart was sheathed in arrows.
5.sharh: Time is the archer and each loss an arrow. They remain where they struck until the heart is enclosed in them. That strange covering will determine what happens to the next arrow.

translation: Now when more arrows strike me,
their heads break on the heads already there.
6.sharh: There is no exposed spot left on the heart. Each fresh point strikes metal. The earlier wounds have deadened it to what follows, a form of endurance no one would willingly acquire.

translation: It grew easy. I pay misfortunes no heed,
for heeding them has done me no good.
7.sharh: Repeated losses have worn down their power to alarm him. He has also learnt that worrying avails him nothing. The repeated “heed” says in ordinary words what the arrowheads have just shown.

translation: Here is the first man ever to bring news of a death,
for the first woman of such majesty to die.
8.sharh: The bearer of the news breaks through his hard-won composure. So singular is the woman who has died that the man announcing her death seems the first to have had such news to bring.

translation: As though death had never bereaved anyone,
never entered the mind of any creature.
9.sharh: Everyone knows of death, and he has just declared himself used to its wounds. This one loss makes all that knowledge fall away. Even the thought of dying seems new.

translation: May the blessing of God our Creator be perfume
on that face shrouded in beauty.
10.sharh: He asks that God's mercy be the fragrance used in preparing her for burial. Her own beauty supplies the shroud. Two familiar funeral rites become a blessing spoken over her face.

translation: On her who lay hidden for modesty's sake before the earth,
and before the grave in the nobility of her ways.
11.sharh: The repeated “on” continues the blessing. The poet borrows the language of burial for her life, when the privacy she kept and the dignity of her conduct already sheltered her from view.

translation: That face has a body deep in the earth.
Our memory of it is fresh as it wears away.
12.sharh: The body changes in the earth, while the memory of it renews itself among the living. The Arabic puts “fresh” beside “worn” and makes each true of the same person in a different respect.

translation: No one among all creatures lives for ever.
The world itself is on its way to an end.
13.sharh: His consolation widens from one person's life to the life of the world. Even the place we hope to remain in is passing away.

translation: What comforts me is that you died a death
women living and women long gone would have wished for.
14.sharh: He can at last address her directly. The wish concerns the circumstances in which she died, her dignity and honour still hers. He imagines women from other generations sharing it with those who survive her.

translation: You went without once seeing such a bitter day
that the soul would welcome its departure.
15.sharh: The death lamented at the start of the verse becomes, at its end, a death someone in distress might be glad of. She was spared the kind of day that could make a soul long to leave the body.

translation: May a morning cloud water your resting place,
as generous with its rain as your hand with gifts.
16.sharh: Rain on a grave is an old wish in Arabic elegy. His measure of a good shower is the dead woman's own generosity. Others once came to her hand for a gift, and now he asks the cloud to give in its turn.

1.1.2.head: المَشرَفِيَّة
1.1.2.meaning: Mashrafi swords, fine blades associated with the Masharif on the approaches to Syria. The adjective stands for the swords.

1.1.3.head: العَوالي
1.1.3.meaning: The upper parts of spear shafts, used here for the whole lances.

1.2.2.head: المَنون
1.2.2.meaning: Death, or time in its power to bring death.

2.1.1.head: اِرتَبَطَ
2.1.1.meaning: To keep horses tethered and ready.

2.1.2.head: السَّوابِق
2.1.2.meaning: Horses swift enough to outrun the rest.

2.1.3.head: مُقرَبة
2.1.3.meaning: A prized horse kept close to its owner's dwelling, tended and ready.

2.2.4.head: خَبَب
2.2.4.meaning: A horse's trot. Giving that gait to the nights makes their pursuit visible.

2.2.5.head: لَيلة
2.2.5.meaning: Nights. The reciter stretches the first syllable and drops the first y, so the word sounds like al-lali. The editions give al-layali, the form the image and metre require.

3.2.5.head: الوِصال
3.2.5.meaning: Union with the beloved. Here it is lasting union with the world.

4.2.5.head: خَيال
4.2.5.meaning: The likeness of an absent loved one visiting a sleeper in a dream.

5.2.3.head: غِشاء
5.2.3.meaning: A covering or sheath enclosing something.

5.2.5.head: نِبال
5.2.5.meaning: Arrows, here the losses left lodged in the heart.

7.1.4.head: الرَّزايا
7.1.4.meaning: Calamities. The Arabic returns to the same root used for the losses two verses earlier.

8.1.3.head: النّاعي
8.1.3.meaning: A bearer of the news of a death.

8.2.2.head: مَيتَة
8.2.2.meaning: A woman who has died. A transmitted reading with a different first vowel means the manner of dying.

9.1.4.head: فَجَعَ
9.1.4.meaning: To bereave someone by the loss of a life.

10.1.4.head: حَنوط
10.1.4.meaning: Hanut, aromatic substances used on the body or shroud in preparing the dead for burial.

11.1.5.head: صَون
11.1.5.meaning: Guarding from view. It describes the privacy she had in life.

11.2.2.head: اللَّحد
11.2.2.meaning: Lahd, a burial niche in the side of a grave, here standing for the grave itself.

11.2.5.head: الخِلال
11.2.5.meaning: Qualities of character or habitual ways of acting.

12.2.2.head: ذِكر
12.2.2.meaning: “Our remembrance of him”, with the pronoun referring back to the bodily person. The unvowelled letters can also suggest the verb “we remembered him”.

12.2.4.head: بالٍ
12.2.4.meaning: Wearing away or decaying. The rhyme retains the final long vowel.

13.2.3.head: آلَ
13.2.3.meaning: To come to something in the end.

14.1.3-4.head: ماتَ
14.1.3-4.meaning: “You died.” The masculine form heard here may refer back to “person”, a masculine word in Arabic. Ibn al-Iflili gives the feminine form. Both address the prince’s mother.

14.2.3.head: الخَوالي
14.2.3.meaning: Women of earlier generations who have passed away.

15.1.2-3.head: رَأى
15.1.2-3.meaning: “You did not see.” He prolongs the final a of the masculine verb, a form allowed in verse. Ibn al-Iflili gives the feminine taray. Both readings fill the same metrical foot.

15.2.4.head: الزَّوال
15.2.4.meaning: Departure, here the soul leaving the body at death.

16.1.2.head: مَثوى
16.1.2.meaning: A resting place or dwelling, here her grave.

16.1.3.meaning: A rain cloud that comes in the morning.

16.2.2.head: نَوال
16.2.2.meaning: A gift freely given, or the act of giving it.
